target: Le sienta bien ese color.
english: That color looks good on her.
tip: Le sienta bien works like gustar: ese color is the subject and le marks the person – literally 'that color sits well to her'.

target: ¿Le diste de comer al perro?
english: Did you feed the dog?
tip: Spanish has no everyday verb 'to feed' – you 'give of eating': 'diste de comer al perro' = you gave the dog (something) to eat.

target: Ella está enferma desde el lunes.
english: She's been sick since Monday.
tip: Está enferma desde el lunes uses plain present where English needs 'has been.' Spanish logic: she is sick right now, and desde just points back to when it started.

target: El lunes empiezo un curso nuevo.
english: On Monday I start a new course.
tip: No 'on' needed: 'El lunes empiezo' – the article alone means 'on Monday'. Singular el lunes = this Monday; plural los lunes = every Monday.

target: Recoge tu cuarto antes de salir.
english: Tidy up your room before you go out.
tip: After antes de comes a bare infinitive: antes de salir, literally 'before to-go-out.' English 'before leaving' tempts you toward a gerund Spanish never uses here.

target: Nos queda una semana de vacaciones.
english: We have one week of vacation left.
tip: In nos queda una semana, the week is the subject – 'a week remains to us.' That's why the verb is queda: quedar agrees with what's left, not with who has it.

target: ¿Cuál es la dirección de la oficina?
english: What is the office address?
tip: '¿Qué es la dirección?' would ask what an address IS – a definition. To pick out a specific one, Spanish switches to 'Cuál es la dirección'.

target: Se parecen mucho el padre y el hijo.
english: The father and son look very much alike.
tip: "Parecerse" = to resemble each other. Reciprocal: "Nos parecemos" = We look alike.

target: Me sale más barato comprar online.
english: It works out cheaper for me to buy online.
tip: Salir here isn't 'to leave' – sale barato means the deal 'comes out' cheap, like a bill totaling up. Me marks who it's cheap for: buying online comes out cheaper for me.

target: ¿Cuánto tardarás en preparar el informe?
english: How long will it take you to prepare the report?
tip: English has no verb for 'take time' – Spanish does: tardar. ¿Cuánto tardarás en preparar...? = how long will you take? And it's always tardar EN + infinitive.

target: No coja un taxi sin taxímetro.
english: Don't take a taxi without a meter.
tip: 'Coja' (from coger, to take) is normal in Spain – but coger is crude slang in much of Latin America. There, say 'tomar un taxi' instead.

target: ¿Cuánto tardas en llegar a la oficina?
english: How long does it take you to get to the office?
tip: Tardar takes en where English says 'take TO': tardas en llegar. Learn it as one chunk – tardar en + infinitive – and you'll never be tempted to translate that 'to' as a.

target: Este autobús para en todas las paradas.
english: This bus stops at every stop.
tip: This para isn't the preposition 'for' – it's the verb parar: el autobús para, the bus stops. A subject sitting right before para is your clue something is stopping.

target: ¿Qué vas a hacer este fin de semana?
english: What are you going to do this weekend?
tip: Vas a hacer: conjugated ir + a + bare verb. That little a is the glue – skip it and the sentence breaks. Spaniards use this far more than actual future-tense endings.

target: Nos falta un documento para cerrar el contrato.
english: We're missing one document to close the contract.
tip: Faltar: nos falta – we're missing/lacking. Works like gustar.

target: Nos quedan dos días para entregar el proyecto.
english: We have two days left to hand in the project.
tip: Quedar: nos quedan – we have... left. Plural agrees with 'dos días'.

target: Las lentejas están un poco sosas, necesitan más especias.
english: The lentils are a bit bland, they need more spices.
tip: 'Estar' for temporary states and taste: 'están sosas' = they taste bland. Compare: 'son buenas' (generally good) vs 'están buenas' (taste good now).

target: Hay que barrer el suelo, está lleno de migas.
english: The floor needs sweeping, it's full of crumbs.
tip: 'Hay que + infinitive' = one must / you have to (impersonal obligation). 'Hay que barrer' = you have to sweep. Different from 'tener que' (personal).

target: El compañero en quien más confío está de vacaciones.
english: The colleague I trust the most is on vacation.
tip: 'En quien' = in whom. After prepositions, use 'quien' for people: 'el compañero en quien confío' = the colleague I trust in.

target: Me gusta ducharme con agua caliente después de hacer ejercicio.
english: I like showering with hot water after exercising.
tip: "Me gusta ducharme" – when gustar is followed by an infinitive, use singular "gusta" (not gustan). The infinitive acts as the subject.

target: No pienso dar mi brazo a torcer en este tema.
english: I'm not going to give in on this issue.
tip: You won't 'give your arm to be twisted': 'dar mi brazo a torcer' pictures losing an arm-wrestle. Refusing to = standing firm, not giving in.

target: Ella tiene los ojos verdes y pecas en la nariz.
english: She has green eyes and freckles on her nose.
tip: Physical descriptions with 'tener': 'tiene los ojos verdes' = she has green eyes. Spanish uses the article 'los' with body parts.

target: ¿Te suena este nombre?
english: Does this name ring a bell?
tip: "Sonar" = to ring a bell / sound familiar. "Me suena" = It sounds familiar to me. Uses gustar-like construction.

target: Me duele la cabeza.
english: My head hurts.
tip: 'Doler' works like 'gustar': the body part is the subject. 'Me duele la cabeza' = My head hurts (lit. the head hurts to me). Plural: 'me duelen los pies.'

target: El día está nublado.
english: The sky is cloudy.
tip: "El día" is masculine – an exception. "Buenos días" (good days) shows the masculine adjective form.

target: La radio no funciona.
english: The radio doesn't work.
tip: "La radio" – feminine because it's short for "la radioemisora." Gender follows the full word.

target: Soy ingeniero de software.
english: I'm a software engineer.
tip: In Spanish, no article before professions: Soy ingeniero (not Soy un ingeniero).

target: Le cuesta mucho madrugar.
english: Getting up early is hard for him.
tip: Costar: le cuesta – it's hard for him/her. Works like gustar.

target: Nos toca pagar a nosotros.
english: It's our turn to pay.
tip: Toca here isn't 'touch' – nos toca means 'it falls to us': it's our turn. The a nosotros at the end doubles down: it's OUR turn to pay, nobody else's.

target: Me encantó la comida local.
english: I loved the local food.
tip: "Encantar" works like "gustar": the thing loved is the subject. "Me encantó" = it enchanted me.
